selected.evidence: اختتم في مدينة حلب السورية معرض المهن الحرفية والتراثية القديمة، الذي أُقيم تحت شعار "لكل حرفة تاريخ يُروى"، بمشاركة حرفيين وفنانين وأصحاب مشروعات سعوا إلى إحياء الحرف المهددة بالاندثار، وتطوير منتجاتها بما يجمع بين الأصالة والحداثة، ونقل خبراتها إلى الأجيال الجديدة. وجاء المعرض في إطار مشروع "صون"، الذي ركز على المهن التراثية الحلبية، بهدف الحفاظ على هذا الإرث الثقافي غير المادي، وتعريف الأجيال الجديدة بالحرف القديمة التي ارتبطت بتاريخ المدينة وحياة سكانها، فضلا عن مساعدة العاملين فيها على تطوير مشروعاتهم وتحويل مهاراتهم التقليدية إلى فرص عمل مستدامة. وقالت مديرة المشروع روميسة شيخ، إن العمل بدأ باستقطاب المستفيدين وفق معايير محددة، مع تخصيص النسبة الكبرى من المشاركين للنساء، مقابل 20% للرجال، بهدف مساعدة النساء اللواتي يمارسن الحرف التراثية في المنازل على الانتقال إلى ريادة الأعمال، وتوسيع نطاق أعمالهن لتصل إلى الأسواق. وأوضحت أن المشاركات خضعن لدورات تدريبية تناولت التسويق والتسعير الرقمي، وآليات ترخيص المشروعات، وبناء هوية بصرية مميزة لكل مشروع، بما يساعد صاحبات الحرف على تقديم منتجاتهن بصورة أكثر احترافية والوصول إلى شرائح أوسع من الزبائن. وأضافت شيخ أن المشروع نظم جولات في أسواق حلب القديمة للتعرف إلى تاريخ الحرف وطبيعة ممارستها، قبل إقامة المعرض الختامي على مدى 3 ليال، في موقع اُختير بمحيط قلعة حلب ، بما يتناسب مع الهوية التاريخية للمكان وطبيعة المبادرة التي تمحورت حول التراث وسبل الحفاظ عليه. وتراوحت أعمار المشاركين بين 17 و60 عاما، في دلالة على اهتمام فئات عمرية مختلفة بالحرف التقليدية، ورغبة أجيال جديدة في تعلمها وتطويرها. ومن بين المشاركين في المعرض الفنان التشكيلي والنحات على الخشب أحمد هنداوي الذي عمل على إحياء هذه الحرفة التي باتت مهددة بالاندثار، من خلال إدخالها إلى مجالي الديكور والخط العربي، وتقديم أعمال جمعت بين التقنيات التقليدية واللمسات الفنية الحديثة. وأوضح هنداوي أنه سعى إلى نقل النحت على الخشب من الاستخدامات التقليدية المرتبطة بالأثاث إلى إنتاج قطع فنية يمكن اقتناؤها بوصفها لوحات تزين المنازل، بما يمنح الحرفة أبعادا جمالية جديدة ويسهم في الحفاظ على جانب من تراث حلب الصناعي والفني. وأشار إلى أن المدينة كانت رائدة في مجال النحت على الخشب خلال الفترة الممتدة من سبعينيات القرن الماضي إلى تسعينياته، معربا عن أمله في استعادة هذه المكانة، ليس من خلال إقامة المعارض فحسب، بل عبر إنشاء أماكن متخصصة لتعليم الحرفة وتحويلها إلى مادة دراسية أو منهج تدريبي يتيح للشباب تعلمها وتطويرها وإضافة أفكار جديدة إليها. بدورها، عرضت الحرفية المتخصصة في المكرمية رغد وزان تجربتها في تطوير هذه الحرفة التراثية وتوسيع استخداماتها. وأوضحت أن المكرمية ارتبطت تاريخيا بصناعة شبكات الصيد لدى البحارة، الذين كانوا يستغلون رحلاتهم الطويلة في إنجاز قطع يدوية، فيما اشتهرت في حلب باستخدامها في صناعة حاملات النباتات. وقالت رغد إنها عملت على تطوير منتجات المكرمية لتشمل الديكورات والمستلزمات المنزلية المتنوعة، وإعادة إدخالها إلى البيوت الحلبية، لما تمنحه من إحساس بالدفء والنعومة، فضلا عن تعريف الشباب والأطفال بتاريخ الحرفة وتشجيعهم على ابتكار تصاميم جديدة مستوحاة منها. وأبدت إحدى زائرات المعرض اعتزازها باستمرار الحرف اليدوية في المدينة، بعدما اعتقد كثيرون أنها مهددة بالاختفاء، مشيدة بالدعم الذي يحظى به الحرفيون وبالدقة الفنية التي ظهرت في المنتجات المعروضة. وقالت إن النحت على الخشب كان من أبرز الأعمال التي لفتت انتباهها، لما يتسم به من دقة وتفاصيل فنية تعكس روح الحرفي الذي أنجز القطعة، معربة عن أملها أن تصل المنتجات التراثية الحلبية إلى الأسواق الخارجية، بما يعزز حضور المدينة بوصفها مركزا عريقا للحرف والأصالة. وشكل المعرض مساحة لعرض المهارات التقليدية أمام الجمهور، وفرصة لربط الحرفيين بالأسواق الحديثة، في محاولة للحفاظ على الموروث الحرفي الحلبي وضمان استمراره عبر الأجيال، مع تطويره بما يتناسب مع متطلبات الحياة المعاصرة.

selected.headline: Cries of forgotten farmers: No compensation on Accra-Kumasi Expressway - Graphic Online
selected.evidence: I write anonymously on behalf of hundreds of desperate farmers whose livelihoods have been impaired due to the construction of the Accra-Kumasi Expressway. Months ago, officials cleared our farms, destroying our cocoa, food crops and oil palms. We stepped aside willingly because we were promised prompt, fair compensation. While the media recently reported that a first tranche of payments was made to over 450 farmers, a massive, forgotten number of us have received absolutely nothing. Our lands are gone, we have no alternative incomes, and our children's school fees are due. When we try to ask for updates, we are met with total silence. The Ministry of Roads and Highways, the Ghana Highway Authority and the Land Valuation Division have become completely unreachable. Development should not destroy the citizens it claims to serve. You cannot take a farmer’s only source of survival and abandon them. We appeal to the media to investigate this delay. We urge the Minister of Roads and Highways and the project coordinators to break their silence and immediately publish a clear, transparent payment schedule for those of us left behind.

selected.headline: NATO commander says the alliance does not want war but is 'ready to fight tonight'
selected.evidence: Gen. Alexus Grynkewich aims to send a clear signal to the Kremlin that the alliance will resist any attack. NATO’s top commander U.S. Gen. Alexus Grynkewich on Monday vowed to block, blunt and break any Russian attack as part of a new “Theory of Victory,” and underlined that alliance troops would fight even if U.S. forces were engaged elsewhere. Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum, Grynkewich outlined how the 32-member alliance would respond to an invasion of NATO territory as concerns grow that Russia could be capable of attacking a NATO member by the end of the decade . “Our alliance exists to preserve peace,” he said, “but let there be no doubt: should war come, we will block, blunt any attack, and then, if it does not cease, we will break the forces conducting aggression against us.” The rare intervention by the four-star general to discuss a military blueprint underscores NATO’s effort to deter Russia. It is also aimed at sending a message of NATO unity after a grueling year for the alliance, which was rocked by Donald Trump’s threats to annex Greenland and infighting over the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran . Under the three-part blueprint, NATO would initially use land-based troops — buttressed by air, naval, cyber and space capabilities — to stop an assault, targeting attacking forces and preventing them from seizing territory, Grynkewich said. NATO would then use sensors and autonomous systems among other capabilities to “overwhelm enemy formations … and their advance,” he said, before using “highly effective precision munitions” and unmanned systems if necessary to “break the [enemy] warfighting system” and “everything that supports” it. Lithuanian Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas said the theory laid out by Grynkewich “will send a strong message to our adversaries that we are going to defend ourselves.” NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Europe said he does “not assess that conflict is imminent or inevitable.” But “we will … ensure any attack against any ally proves utterly futile.” The speech describes a more forceful response if a foe attacks, but its credibility depends on allies having the forces, infrastructure, and coordination to implement the plan. Asked whether the plan factored in a scenario where the U.S. was engaged elsewhere, Grynkewich said: “It absolutely does account for that, and in fact, it must.” Under Trump, the U.S. has sought to refocus its military on other priorities such as the Indo-Pacific, homeland security and the Western Hemisphere. U.S. ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker said in Warsaw on Monday that Europe only ranks fourth among Washington’s strategic concerns. The Pentagon has already cut its contributions to NATO crisis forces and is set to unveil a review of U.S. forces in Europe by the end of the year. “No one should question the commitment of the United States to this alliance,” Grynkewich argued, but added that “ultimately, it's a political decision about who's providing troops where.” Camille Grand, NATO's former assistant secretary-general for defense investment, said the plan was “a very deliberate effort” to signal that the alliance would be ready to fight with or without large-scale involvement of U.S. forces. “For my country, fighting with Russians is with or without Americans,” said a separate senior European defense official, who was granted anonymity to speak freely. “We expect them to come, but if they won’t, we will fight anyway.” Grand added that the blueprint is also an indication that NATO is ready to take a bolder approach toward Moscow by threatening the destruction of its war machine even deep behind the front lines. That comes as Moscow sent a letter to NATO last month threatening to use its nuclear arsenal if the alliance tried to isolate its Kaliningrad exclave. Grynkewich warned that NATO would be ready to respond — even with its nuclear arsenal. “Should an adversary threaten escalation by saber-rattling, or should one actually decide to escalate during conflict, it will not fracture our alliance,” he said. “We should take comfort in our ability to deliver mass effects and the implicit warning that we could match any enemy move up the escalation ladder.” Italy is hosting NATO’s annual nuclear exercise, which starts next week. Insurgent far-right parties are seizing on cost-of-living grievances and waning support for defense spending. Police said the two men received instructions and materials to make a homemade bomb for possible use on Jewish targets. Three missile and two drones entered Moldovan airspace and caused collateral damage in the country, local authorities said.

selected.headline: Fear and uncertainty for civilians as Yemen’s capital comes under attack | Houthis
selected.evidence: Sanaa has come under intense bombing since the Yemeni government announced a campaign to take the capital from the Houthis. Sanaa, Yemen – At midnight on Tuesday, air strikes rattled the Yemeni capital Sanaa, a city that has been mostly spared bombing since a truce was announced between the internationally recognised government and the Houthis in 2023. The head of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, Rashid al-Alimi, had recently announced a new military offensive was being launched, named Operation Dawn of Yemen, to take Sanaa from the Houthis, who have held the city since September 2014. Government ground forces remain hundreds of miles away from the capital and embroiled in fighting with the Houthis on Yemen’s west coast and around Taiz. This means attacks on Houthi positions in Sanaa must come from the air, but the air campaign has caused civilian casualties. An air strike on Monday hit a location in the Sa’wan area of Sanaa governorate, killing a child and wounding seven other civilians. The Yemeni government has pledged to continue its attacks until it achieves its objectives, notably the recapture of Sanaa. Regardless of the political opinions of Yemenis in the capital, most fear their city, far from the front lines, will become a war zone once again. Strong memories remain of the Saudi-led coalition’s Operation Decisive Storm , launched against the Houthis in March 2015, which saw hundreds of civilians in Sanaa killed in air strikes. Since the start of the new Yemeni government offensive, dozens of strikes have hit the capital, including an attack on Sanaa’s international airport, which killed two workers. Both operations were aimed at Houthi sites. Ghamadan Abood, a 30-year-old courier and Sanaa resident, said the new wave of attacks on the city has heightened fear among residents. “When I learned about the new operation on Sunday, my feeling of security shrank,” he told Al Jazeera. “At any time and anywhere, air strikes may hit, and civilians could become the next casualties.” On Monday, Abood was travelling on his bike when air strikes hit Sa’wan, just two kilometres from where he was. With Houthi military facilities believed to be positioned in the city, and the government sometimes hitting residential areas, the bombing highlights the vulnerability of civilians in Sanaa. “The strikes could be aimed at missile launch pads, military equipment or facilities, but some of these facilities could be near neighbourhoods, farms or roads. So, innocent people could be killed, injured or left terrified,” Abood said. Saudi Arabia, which supports the Yemeni government, has also come under repeated missile attacks by the Houthis, including two strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, the latest on Saturday killing 12 people . On Tuesday, the Saudi-led coalition said Sanaa, Saada, and Amran were among the primary sources of Houthi missile threats. The coalition has noted that ongoing military operations are aimed at curbing the group’s ability to launch missiles on the kingdom. More than 200,000 people have been displaced since fighting in Yemen escalated in recent weeks, according to the International Organization for Migration. Most of those forced to leave their homes have come from Taiz governorate in southwestern Yemen, where the most intense ground fighting between government and Houthi forces has taken place. Saleh Ayidh, a 50-year-old resident of Sanaa and father of five, fears the new air strikes will also force people from their homes in the north. “Today, we see Sanaa as a safe place and distant from the front lines. For me, no place is safe in Yemen, particularly in the north, and war can spread anywhere,” he told Al Jazeera. At the start of the Saudi-led coalition’s operation against the Houthis in March 2015, Ayidh’s family left the city for a home in the countryside. They lived there for six months, far from the assault on the Yemeni capital. “Now we do not know what will happen to us. We will decide whether we need to leave the city if the air strikes keep intensifying,” Ayidh said. “Without safety, life is hard.” The recent air strikes are widely viewed in Sanaa as a sign that war has returned to the capital, prompting residents to stock up on food and fuel. When Operation Decisive Storm began in 2015, the cost of goods and fuel rose due to disruption to logistics and panic buying. The same trend is being seen again in Sanaa after the recent resumption of hostilities. Grocery owner Nashwan, 24, has boosted his inventory of essentials such as rice, cheese, milk, biscuits, cooking oil and sugar, before they become too difficult to find. He also stocked up on petrol, buying 100 litres to use for his minibus if a fuel crisis hits the capital. “These commodities may become expensive in the coming days. If the war keeps escalating, buying them would cost me more,” Nashwan said. “I do not want to feel the impact of the war immediately.” Any road closures or a decline in imports caused by the war and a Saudi naval siege on Houthi areas will present major challenges for civilians. “Rising prices of food and fuel are a real worry for the entire population amid the war and will worsen the humanitarian situation in Yemen,” Wafiq Saleh, executive director of the Taiz Centre for Yemeni-Gulf Studies, told Al Jazeera. Last week, the UN World Food Programme warned that three-quarters of families in parts of Yemen were going hungry. There are fears an escalation of the fighting will lead to a more intense food crisis across Yemen, which the WFP has already described as “absolutely devastating”. Despite the optimism of the internationally recognised government when announcing Operation Dawn of Yemen, few in Sanaa believe it has the ability to recapture the capital from the Houthis any time soon. selected.headline: Russian cluster munition strike kills three generations of Ukrainian family, police say
selected.evidence: Russian cluster munition strike kills three generations of Ukrainian family, police say A 13-year-old girl, her 36-year-old mother and 62-year-old grandmother were killed when a Russian rocket struck their home in the village of Cherkaske in Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast on Oct. 12, Ukrainian police and regional authorities reported . The attack occurred at approximately 11:15 a.m. Russian forces used a Smerch multiple-launch rocket system equipped with a cluster warhead, according to Donetsk Oblast Governor Vadym Filashkin. Four other people were injured, including an 18-year-old man and three older men, police said. Nearby homes were also damaged. “One strike destroyed the lives of an entire family,” Filashkin wrote on Telegram. The governor accused Russian forces of deliberately targeting residential areas with cluster munitions to inflict maximum civilian casualties. He renewed his appeal to families with children to evacuate from dangerous areas of Donetsk Oblast rather than wait for another attack. According to regional authorities, 272 people, including 41 children, were evacuated from frontline areas of the oblast over the preceding 24 hours. We work for you and thanks to you. Be our friend

selected.headline: A headscarf at the school gates: the dispute over hijab and the future of Azerbaijani girls
selected.evidence: In October 1901, the Alexandrinsky Russian-Muslim School for Girls — the first Muslim girls’ school in the Caucasus — opened in Baku with funding from oil industrialist and philanthropist Haji Zeynalabdin Taghiyev. Dressed in black, Taghiyev stands in the centre among the pupils and teachers of the Baku Muslim Girls’ School. New school uniform requirements have once again brought Azerbaijan’s secular tradition into conflict with the religious beliefs of some families. But behind the dispute over clothing lies a simpler question: how can every girl be kept in education? In videos shared on social media, schoolgirls wearing headscarves leave school in tears: they have been denied entry to lessons. The voices of the pupils themselves are heard far less often in the public debate than declarations about their future. A headscarf alone cannot reveal whether a girl wears it out of personal conviction, family custom or pressure. Nor can her tears establish every cause of the conflict. That is why any solution must begin with a conversation with the child, rather than assigning someone else’s position to her. For some parents, what is happening has already become a question of access to education. One parent in Sumgayit told AzadlıqRadiosu : “Our children are not being allowed into school because of our religious beliefs.” This is a parent’s testimony, rather than a fact established by a court. But it identifies these families’ central fear: a clothing requirement could mean missed lessons. The current dispute gained fresh momentum following Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 309 of September 21, 2026. It added a prohibition to the school uniform rules on clothing elements that undermine the uniform’s consistency and do not comply with the principle of secular general education. Yet the word “hijab” does not appear in the document. Questions of compliance have been assigned to schools’ pedagogical councils , while parents are required to ensure that their children follow the rules. National dress, or elements of it, may be worn at events dedicated to Azerbaijan’s history and culture with the permission of the pedagogical council. The distinction between the resolution’s wording and its practical application matters. The document establishes clothing requirements, but contains no explicit provision barring pupils from lessons specifically for wearing hijab. Each such case therefore requires separate examination: who made the decision, on what grounds, in what form, and how can the family appeal? The official position of education authorities centres on order and equality. Announcing checks on uniform compliance, the Baku City Education Department said the aim was to create a disciplined, orderly and equal educational environment. School management is responsible for oversight, while disputed questions are referred to pedagogical councils. There is an understandable educational logic to this position. A common uniform can reduce displays of economic differences, simplify school rules and reinforce a sense of belonging to the same community. But a question remains: if the rest of a pupil’s clothing meets the prescribed uniform requirements, must a headscarf be prohibited to achieve those goals? There is no single interpretation within the education community. In comments to Referans Media , education expert Elchin Efendi stresses the need to comply with school uniform requirements and prevent religious views from being imposed on other pupils. His colleague Ramin Nuraliyev points to the absence of an explicit ban on covering the head. “A girl wearing a headscarf does not mean a departure from the school uniform,” he told AzEdu. An important distinction lies here: personal religious expression and pressure on others require different assessments. Appearance alone does not prove an attempt to impose beliefs. In Azerbaijan, a dispute over women’s head coverings inevitably becomes a conversation about history. Some see contemporary hijab as a return to religious practice; others see the spread of clothing that differs from the familiar appearance of mothers and grandmothers. A historical distinction exists, but it is difficult to capture in the formula “there was no hijab before”. Hijab does not denote one unchanging style of clothing. In contemporary everyday speech, the word often refers to a scarf covering the hair and neck; in broader religious usage, it refers to standards for covering the body. The kelaghayi, an ordinary headscarf and the chador are specific garments that could carry cultural, practical and religious significance at the same time. Azerbaijani tradition was diverse. The national portal describes kelaghayi, other scarves and head coverings , their combinations and regional characteristics. Sometimes the hair was first gathered beneath one covering, with a silk scarf tied over it. Fabrics, patterns and ways of wearing them varied. The observation that younger women wore brightly coloured scarves and older women darker ones is reflected in materials from Azerbaijan’s National Commission for UNESCO . But colour also depended on the occasion: a wedding, mourning, a celebration or everyday life. UNESCO, which added the art of making and wearing kelaghayi to its intangible cultural heritage list in 2014, links the tradition to both cultural identity and religious customs. The chador, also called a charshab, differed from a headscarf: it was a larger covering that concealed the head and much of the body. Photographs and paintings from the 19th and early 20th centuries therefore need to be read carefully. Urban clothing could differ from rural dress, festive clothing from everyday attire, and the costume of one locality from that of another. These images testify to the diversity of the past. They do not justify declaring a single way of dressing the compulsory expression of national identity. The emancipation of Azerbaijani women cannot be reduced to the moment when the chador was removed
